issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette:
Tane, a 48-year-old man of Oceanic descent, had been living with the shadows of his past for nearly three years since the night that changed everything. The memories of that traumatic event loomed large in his life, overshadowing ordinary moments and consuming his thoughts. He had been working late on a job site, the sun setting as he left the roof of a commercial building, when he was ambushed. The assailant was someone he had thought was a friend, someone he had trusted. The violation was brutal and left him feeling stripped of control and safety. Since then, Tane had struggled to reconcile the vividness of that night with the mundane reality of his daily life. 

As he moved through the weeks following the assault, Tane began to notice how certain sounds triggered an avalanche of memories. The roar of motorcycles on the road would send a cold shiver down his spine, pulling him back to the moment when he felt trapped, powerless under the weight of someone else's aggression. He often found himself tensing up whenever he heard that distinctive engine growl, and he couldn’t help but feel a surge of panic that left him breathless. He would avoid walking near busy streets, crossing the road to steer clear of any bike that might pass by. The avoidance felt necessary, as if he were shielding himself from a recurring nightmare.

Tane's response to his trauma extended beyond just avoiding triggering situations; he became hyper-vigilant, always scanning his environment for threats. News stories about similar assaults would cut through him like a knife, each headline serving as a reminder of his own experience. He would feel the familiar knot of anxiety tightening in his chest, a visceral reminder of the violation he had endured. To cope, he would scroll past these stories, promising himself it was for the best, but deep down, he feared that ignoring the truth would only allow it to fester. 

In the months that followed, Tane developed habits that seemed harmless at first but soon became his lifelines. He began to avoid physical stress, telling himself that he needed to keep his body safe. Roofer by trade, he found himself hesitant to take on jobs that required heavy lifting or strenuous activity. He would often take the easier tasks, even if it meant earning less money. He found solace in the idea that if he could control his body’s exertion, he could also control the flood of emotions that threatened to overwhelm him. It was a balancing act, one that kept him tethered to a sense of safety, but it also began to erode his confidence as a hard worker.

In an effort to maintain that illusion of control, Tane began to restrict his eating. Food became a means of asserting dominance over his own body, a way to feel powerful in a life that constantly felt out of control. He meticulously tracked his meals, counting calories and obsessively planning everything he consumed. Yet, with each passing day, he felt more disconnected from the joy of eating, replacing it with an oppressive sense of duty. He had come to believe that if he could just keep his body in check, perhaps he could avoid the emotional upheaval that haunted him.

Additionally, Tane found it easier to drown himself in work. He filled his days with a relentless pursuit of busyness, taking on extra hours and multiple jobs. He believed that staying occupied would keep his mind off the memories that threatened to engulf him. But as he pushed himself harder, he felt an unshakeable weight of grief whenever he couldn’t suppress the images of that night. There were moments when the emotional intensity hit him without warning, leaving him breathless, crying in silence as he recalled the loss of safety and the innocence that had been taken from him. 

His wife, Aroha, noticed the changes in him, but every time she tried to talk, Tane would retreat further into himself. He loved her dearly but felt suffocated by the weight of his own grief. He had come to believe that sharing his pain would only hurt her, so he kept it hidden, crafting a façade of normalcy that felt increasingly impossible to maintain. 

Finally, it was a particularly vivid news report that pushed Tane to the edge. He felt the crushing wave of grief and despair wash over him, and for the first time since the assault, he couldn't contain it. That night, he turned to Aroha, tears streaming down his face, and confessed everything—the trauma, the avoidance, the shame. It was in that moment of vulnerability that he realized he could no longer carry the burden alone. 

Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Tane felt a mix of fear and hope. He was terrified of confronting the memories that had haunted him for so long, but he also yearned for a sense of peace he had lost. He hoped that through this journey, he might reclaim a part of himself that had been buried under layers of grief and self-protection.
